name: American Indian Movement
info: The American Indian Movement (AIM) is a grassroots movement founded in Minneapolis in July 1968 to address poverty, discrimination and police brutality against American Indians, and later treaty rights, land and the preservation of Indigenous cultures.

facts.where: Minneapolis and St Paul, Minnesota; the Pine Ridge Reservation in South Dakota; Washington, D.C.; Alcatraz Island; chapters across the United States, with ties to Indigenous peoples outside it
facts.period: founded in Minneapolis in 1968; occupations and marches 1969 to 1972; Wounded Knee 1973; the Longest Walk 1978; split into two groups 1993; active today
facts.figures: Dennis J. Banks (Ojibwe), co-founder; Russell Means (Oglala Lakota), co-founder; Leonard Peltier, an organiser convicted of killing two FBI agents; Clyde and Vernon Bellecourt; Anna Mae Aquash, the highest-ranking woman in AIM; Hank Adams, who largely wrote the Twenty Points
facts.outcome: a lasting set of schools, housing, legal and job-training organisations and the International Indian Treaty Council; the 1973 occupation at Wounded Knee drew international attention; leaders were tried and the case dismissed for prosecutorial misconduct; the movement divided in 1993

t: AIM was founded in 1968 by Native American men who had served time in prison together, in a city where thousands of American Indians had moved under the relocation policy of the 1950s.

It used occupations, marches and the press to put treaty rights before the American public, from Alcatraz and Mount Rushmore to the Trail of Broken Treaties in 1972 and the 71-day occupation of Wounded Knee in 1973.

AIM founded schools, housing, job training, legal centres and the International Indian Treaty Council, but violence on Pine Ridge, FBI infiltration and a split in 1993 left it divided into rival groups.
dyk: In 1973 the actor Marlon Brando asked Sacheen Littlefeather to decline his Academy Award for him; she arrived in Apache regalia and read his statement citing the poor treatment of Native Americans in the film industry.
ev: AIM is founded in Minneapolis, and the Minneapolis AIM Patrol is created to monitor police treatment of urban American Indians
On Thanksgiving Day an AIM group seizes the replica of the Mayflower in Boston, and AIM declares Thanksgiving a National Day of Mourning
Members occupy Mount Rushmore for a few days to protest the seizure of the Black Hills, and briefly occupy the headquarters of the Bureau of Indian Affairs in Washington
The Trail of Broken Treaties ends in the occupation of the Bureau of Indian Affairs headquarters, where the Twenty Points are publicised
About 300 Oglala Lakota and AIM activists occupy Wounded Knee, South Dakota, in a siege that lasts 71 days
Two FBI agents, Jack Coler and Ronald Williams, are killed on the Pine Ridge Reservation
The Longest Walk of 3,200 miles ends in Washington, D.C., and Congress passes the American Indian Religious Freedom Act
AIM splits into the Grand Governing Council and the International Confederation of Autonomous Chapters

sections.background:
AIM was organised in Minneapolis in July 1968 by Native American men who had been serving time together in prison. Experiences that several of them shared included boarding school education, military service and the disorienting urban experience. They had been alienated from their traditional backgrounds in part by the Indian Relocation Act of 1956, which supported thousands of American Indians who wanted to move from reservations to cities for work, and by Public Law 280, one of the first major laws of the termination policy. As a result nearly 70% of American Indians left their communal homelands on reservations for urban centres. Many struggled with displacement, and some began to organise in pan-Indian groups. AIM formed in such urban settings at a time of increasing Indian activism.

Older struggles over land lay behind it. In the 1950s many American Indians believed that leases had become too often a way for outsiders to control Indian land, and Wallace “Mad Bear” Anderson (Tuscarora) resisted the planner Robert Moses’s scheme to take tribal land in upstate New York for a hydropower project; the struggle ended in a bitter compromise. Uranium mining on Navajo lands, begun under a federal policy from 1940, left mines that still pollute Navajo communities, and the Navajo believe the federal government violated the Treaty of 1868.
sections.aims:
AIM first set out to address systemic poverty, discrimination and police brutality against American Indians in cities. It soon widened its scope to many Indigenous tribal issues arising from settler colonialism in the Americas: treaty rights, high unemployment, the lack of American Indian subjects in education and the preservation of Indigenous cultures. Its leaders drew inspiration from African American leaders of the Civil Rights Movement and spoke of unemployment, slum housing and racist treatment, while also fighting for treaty rights and the reclamation of tribal land.

The Twenty Points, largely written by the activist and strategist Hank Adams and publicised during the 1972 occupation, summarised its complaints about federal treaties and promises. Twelve of them concerned treaty responsibilities that the protesters believed the United States had failed to fulfil. They asked to restore treaty-making, which Congress ended in 1871, to set up a treaty commission, to review treaty violations and to restore 110 million acres taken from Native Nations. Others called for repeal of Public Law 280, abolition of the Bureau of Indian Affairs, protection of Indian religious freedom and cultural integrity, and improved health, housing, employment and education.

AIM also opposed the use of Indigenous figures as sports mascots and team names, and condemned what its Southwest chapter called in 1984 the “direct attack and theft” of expropriating Indian ceremonies.
sections.events:
AIM used the press as civil rights and antiwar activists did, creating events to win coverage. On Thanksgiving Day 1970 an AIM group seized the replica of the Mayflower in Boston, and in 1971 members occupied Mount Rushmore for a few days, protesting the taking of the Black Hills from the Lakota. In 1971 members also briefly occupied the Bureau of Indian Affairs headquarters in Washington, D.C. In 1972 the Trail of Broken Treaties ended with the occupation, for several days, of the Department of the Interior headquarters, which AIM was alleged to have damaged to the extent of millions of dollars. AIM also took part in the occupation of Alcatraz Island from November 1969 to June 1971, organised by seven Indian movements.

In 1973 AIM was invited to Pine Ridge to help gain justice from law enforcement in border counties and to moderate political factions. On 27 February about 300 Oglala Lakota and AIM activists went to Wounded Knee, the site of the 1890 massacre, and a 71-day siege followed, with the FBI cordoning off the area using U.S. Marshals and later National Guard units. The occupiers declared the Independent Oglala Nation. Gunfire occurred on both sides; in April a Cherokee and a Lakota activist were killed, and the elders ended the occupation. Afterwards 1200 American Indians were arrested.

In 1978 the Longest Walk, 3,200 miles across the country, arrived in Washington, D.C. on 15 July. A second walk of 8,200 miles in 2008 included representatives of more than 100 nations.
sections.people:
Dennis J. Banks, an Ojibwe, co-founded AIM in Minneapolis in 1968 and became one of its most recognisable faces. Russell Means, an Oglala Lakota from the Pine Ridge Reservation, collaborated with Banks to formulate AIM and was a central leader. Leonard Peltier, enrolled in the turtle band Chippewa tribe in North Dakota but also Lakota and Dakota, was an organiser and activist. Clyde Bellecourt and his brother Vernon Bellecourt later led the Grand Governing Council. Louis Bruce (Mohawk/Lakota), the BIA Commissioner, showed his AIM membership card at a meeting in 1971.

Anna Mae Aquash was the highest-ranking woman in AIM. Women had a part in its work: in 1974 Lorelei DeCora Means, Madonna Thunder Hawk, Phyllis Young and Janet McCloud founded Women of All Red Nations (WARN), a women’s movement within AIM, and at Wounded Knee women took up arms to defend the hamlet. The women elders of Pine Ridge encouraged the men to act. Hank Adams wrote most of the Twenty Points. Outside supporters included Marlon Brando, who had Sacheen Littlefeather speak for him at the 1973 Academy Awards, and, for the Longest Walk, Muhammad Ali, Senator Ted Kennedy and Nichidatsu Fujii.
sections.outcomes:
AIM won attention and some concrete results. Occupations drew press coverage, and after Wounded Knee polls showed that Americans were sympathetic to the Indian cause. At the Winter Dam in 1971 AIM helped the Lac Courte Oreilles Ojibwe take over a dam controlled by Northern States Power; the federal government later returned more than 25,000 acres to the tribe. Congress withdrew the bills the Longest Walk opposed and passed the American Indian Religious Freedom Act in 1978. In 1980 the Supreme Court ruled that the federal government had illegally taken the Black Hills; the Oglala Sioux have refused the compensation offered and insist on return of the land. AIM’s Wounded Knee leaders were tried in a Minnesota federal court, which dismissed the case for governmental prosecutorial misconduct.

The movement also met violence and repression. The Department of Justice scrutinised AIM, and the FBI used paid informants. In 1973 at Custer, South Dakota, AIM activists attacked and burned a Chamber of Commerce building, the courthouse and two patrol cars, causing $2 million in damages. More than 60 people died in violent incidents on Pine Ridge in the three years after 1973, an episode called the “Pine Ridge Reign of Terror”. On 26 June 1975 the FBI agents Jack Coler and Ronald Williams were killed there; Butler and Robideau were acquitted, and Peltier was convicted in 1976. Amnesty International has referred to his case under its Unfair Trials category.
sections.legacy:
AIM founded institutions that lasted: the Heart of the Earth School, Little Earth Housing, AIM StreetMedics, the American Indian Opportunities Industrialisation Center, KILI radio, Indian Legal Rights Centers and the International Indian Treaty Council, set up in June 1974, which became a non-governmental organisation with consultative status to the United Nations in 1977. On 13 September 2007 the UN General Assembly adopted the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples; 144 states voted in favour, four against and 11 abstained.

The movement divided. In 1993 it split into the AIM Grand Governing Council, based in Minneapolis, which tends towards a more centralised philosophy, and the International Confederation of Autonomous Chapters, based in Denver, which issued the Edgewood Declaration complaining of authoritarian leadership by the Bellecourts and holds that AIM was always a series of autonomous chapters. In 1999 Russell Means accused Vernon Bellecourt of ordering the killing of Anna Mae Aquash, which Bellecourt denied; Arlo Looking Cloud and John Graham were later convicted of her murder. Peltier, whom many believed had not had a fair trial, was released from federal prison in 2025 on condition of home confinement.

AIM chapters continue to protest, and in 2020 members of a splinter group, AIM Twin Cities, tore down a Columbus statue at the Minnesota State Capitol, an act the Grand Governing Council disowned.

summary: The American Indian Movement was founded in Minneapolis in 1968 by Native American men who had served time together in prison. Through occupations, marches and the siege at Wounded Knee it pressed treaty rights and founded schools and other institutions, and it divided into rival groups in 1993.
references: Dennis Banks and Richard Erdoes, Ojibwa Warrior: Dennis Banks and the Rise of the American Indian Movement (University of Oklahoma Press, 2004)
Vine Deloria Jr., Custer Died for Your Sins: An Indian Manifesto (University of Oklahoma Press, 1988)
Troy R. Johnson, Red Power: The Native American Civil Rights Movement (Chelsea House, 2007)
Joane Nagel, American Indian Ethnic Renewal: Red Power and the Resurgence of Identity and Culture (Oxford University Press, 1996)
Peter Matthiessen, In the Spirit of Crazy Horse (Penguin Books, 1992)
notes: References were meant to be left empty for the editor; I filled five from the article's Bibliography. Replace or empty as preferred.
Contradiction: the article says an FBI agent was left paralysed at Wounded Knee (events summary) and that U.S. Marshal Lloyd Grimm was paralysed (1973 section). I left the paralysis out.
Contradiction: the article says Peltier was released in 2025 and also that he is currently serving two consecutive life sentences. I used the 2025 release only.

The article gives Wounded Knee deaths as a Cherokee and a Lakota killed in April; it also says two others went missing and are believed killed (Ray Robinson, whom the FBI confirmed in 2014 was killed and buried on the reservation, allegedly by AIM members in an argument). Left out for length; the editor may wish to add.
Alcatraz: the article says AIM took part in an occupation organised by seven movements (Nov 1969 to June 1971) and, elsewhere, that it was led by the United Indians of All Tribes; I used the first.
The Mount Rushmore protest is dated 1971 in the article; the Black Hills taking is dated 1877 in one place and after the 1874 gold discovery in another; I gave no year for the taking.

Left out: the Miskito support (1980s), support of Gaddafi in 2011, the Republic of Lakotah, Irish and Welsh commemorations, the 2025 documentary and an unreferenced sentence on Operation Metro Surge; also the mascot-negotiation details.
Peltier's tribe is given as the article writes it ('turtle band Chippewa').
